title: Electric Car and EV Basics
desc: Understand how electric vehicles work, charge, cost and stay safe, and how to advise buyers and fleets honestly.
outcomes: Explain motor, battery, charger and range.
Estimate running cost and charging time.
Judge battery health, safety and resale.
Write a buyer or fleet advice sheet.
task: Produce an advice sheet comparing one EV with one petrol car for a given user, with cost, range, charging and safety notes.
condition: A computer, public specifications, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor. No high-voltage work is done.
standard: Maths is correct and in your currency; assumptions are stated; safety rules for high-voltage parts are included; claims are sourced; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Sales staff, drivers, fleet clerks, technician trainees.
evidence: comparison sheet, charging time sheet, safety notes, advice sheet
modules: How an electric vehicle works
Understand
An electric car swaps the engine, fuel tank and gearbox for a battery, a motor and a controller. Knowing the chain lets you explain every cost and limit later.
Energy flows battery to controller to motor to wheels; braking sends some energy back to the battery.
A motor gives full pull from a standstill, so the car feels quick and quiet with one gear.
A small battery runs lights, screens and cooling; the traction battery drives the wheels.
Fewer moving parts means fewer routine services, but tyres, brakes and suspension still wear.
A 60 kWh car uses about 15 kWh per 100 km. The motor turns about 90 per cent of battery energy into motion; a petrol engine turns about 30 per cent of fuel energy into motion.
Draw the energy chain for one named EV type and mark the loss at each step.
Chain is complete and ordered, losses are shown as percentages, and regenerative braking is explained in one sentence.
Batteries
Understand
The battery is the costliest and most sensitive part. A buyer must read its size, health and warranty.
Capacity is in kWh; usable capacity is lower than the headline number.
Heat, deep discharge and constant fast charging age the battery faster.
Warranty usually states years or kilometres and a minimum health level.
Cold weather cuts range temporarily; hot weather speeds ageing.
A battery with 60 kWh capacity and 90 per cent health holds 54 kWh. A warranty to 70 per cent health after 8 years is a better promise than a warranty with no health level.
Read a sample warranty and list capacity, health level, years and kilometre limit.
All four facts are extracted correctly and one question for the seller is written.
Charging levels and time
Apply
Time to charge depends on power. Home, work and route charging suit different users.
Time in hours = energy needed / charging power, with about 10 per cent loss.
Slow home points give 2 to 7 kW; fast route chargers give 50 kW and more.
Cars limit their own intake as the battery fills, so the last 20 per cent is slow.
Match the charging place to where the car sits longest.
Adding 30 kWh at 7 kW takes 30 / 7 x 1.1 = 4.7 hours, so overnight home charging fits. At 50 kW the same energy takes about 40 minutes.
Calculate charging time for one user at home and at a route charger.
Both times are shown with the formula and the 10 per cent loss; the right place is chosen with a reason.
Running cost comparison
Analyse
Compare fairly: energy, servicing, insurance, tax and the price difference.
Cost per km = price per unit of energy x energy per km.
Add servicing, insurance, tax and parking for both cars.
Include purchase price difference and how many years the user will keep the car.
State clearly what is a measured number and what is an assumption.

A user drives 12,000 km a year (prices are estimates; check your market). Electric: 15 kWh per 100 km at 8 per kWh costs 1.2 per km, 14,400 a year. Petrol: 6 litres per 100 km at 100 per litre costs 6 per km, 72,000 a year. The saving is 57,600 a year.
Build a five-year cost table for one EV and one petrol car.
Totals add up, assumptions are listed, and break-even year is stated.
Real-world range
Evaluate
Label range is measured in set conditions. Real range moves with speed, load, weather and use of air conditioning.
Highway speed and cold weather cut range most.
Heavy loads and hills use more energy; downhill braking gives some back.
Plan with a margin: use about 80 per cent of label range.
Check route chargers before long trips.
A car with 400 km label range gives about 320 km usable. In winter on a highway it may give 250 km. A 280 km trip needs a charging stop.
Plan one trip and decide if a stop is needed.
Margin is applied, weather is considered, and the stop plan names where and how long.
Safety
Apply
High voltage needs respect, from driver to emergency crew.
Orange cables usually mark high voltage; only trained people work on them.
Cars have isolation systems that disconnect the battery in a crash.
Never charge with damaged cables or in standing water.
Fire services need clear information on the car type and battery position.
A flooded car is not touched or charged. It is reported, isolated outdoors and checked by a trained technician before use.
Write a ten-line safety card for a new owner.
Card covers charging, damage, flooding and what to tell responders, in plain words.
Battery end of life
Evaluate
A battery is still valuable when it can no longer power a car.
Below about 70 to 80 per cent health a car battery may serve as home or shop storage.
Recycling recovers metals; collect through approved centres only.
Ask the maker or seller about take-back.
Never dismantle at home.
A battery at 72 per cent health still stores 43 kWh from a 60 kWh pack. It can back up a small shop for years before recycling.
Write a three-step plan for a battery at the end of its car life.
Plan names reuse, recycling route and who is responsible.
Write the advice sheet
Create
Bring the work together as one honest sheet for a named user.
Start with the user: distance, budget, parking, charging access.
Show the cost table, range plan and charging plan.
State one risk and one limit in plain words.
End with a clear recommendation and what would change it.
For a user with home parking, 30 km daily trips and one 300 km trip a month, the sheet recommends the EV and a hire car or a charging stop for the long trip.
Produce the full one-page advice sheet.
All parts are present, numbers are consistent, and a reader can act on it without help.
quiz: What does regen braking do?

Returns some energy to the battery. (Covered in module 1: How an electric vehicle works. To pass that module: Chain is complete and ordered, losses are shown as percentages, and regenerative braking is explained in one sentence.)
Charging time formula?

Energy / power plus losses. (Covered in module 3: Charging levels and time. To pass that module: Both times are shown with the formula and the 10 per cent loss; the right place is chosen with a reason.)
Name a battery ageing factor.
Heat or frequent fast charging. (Covered in module 2: Batteries. To pass that module: All four facts are extracted correctly and one question for the seller is written.)
Who works on orange cables?
Trained technicians. (Covered in module 6: Safety. To pass that module: Card covers charging, damage, flooding and what to tell responders, in plain words.)
What affects range?
Speed, temperature, load, hills. (Covered in module 5: Real-world range. To pass that module: Margin is applied, weather is considered, and the stop plan names where and how long.)
EV running cost steps?
kWh per 100 km x price per kWh. (Covered in module 4: Running cost comparison. To pass that module: Totals add up, assumptions are listed, and break-even year is stated.)
Name an end-of-life option.
Second life or recycling. (Covered in module 7: Battery end of life. To pass that module: Plan names reuse, recycling route and who is responsible.)
Why keep a reserve?
Range varies. (Covered in module 5: Real-world range. To pass that module: Margin is applied, weather is considered, and the stop plan names where and how long.)
What costs besides fuel?
Service, insurance, tax, depreciation. (Covered in module 4: Running cost comparison. To pass that module: Totals add up, assumptions are listed, and break-even year is stated.)
What is usable capacity?
Less than the label capacity. (Covered in module 2: Batteries. To pass that module: All four facts are extracted correctly and one question for the seller is written.)
rubric: Price, tariff and range come from dated sources
Running cost per 100 km worked out for both cars, with assumptions listed
Home charging safety, warranty and insurance points are written down
Points checked with a licensed electrician and the insurer
